
Both recordings showed an overall decline in heart rate. In each, the bi-exponential model had the lowest AICc among the three models tested. Its RMSE was 3.114 bpm for the 7.5-minute recording and 7.944 bpm for the three-hour recording. The fitted curves and AICc results therefore favour the bi-exponential model as the best statistical fit among our candidates.

This finding is consistent with research describing a fast and a slower phase of heart-rate recovery. Those phases are commonly associated with parasympathetic reactivation and sympathetic withdrawal, respectively [@Bartels2018]. A double-exponential model has also fitted recovery data better than a single-exponential model in many participants following maximal exercise, although the result was not consistent for every participant [@Joseph2023]. Other work found that a mono-exponential model can adequately describe recovery in a different exercise context, so the literature does not establish one model as best for every protocol [@BartelsFerreira2015].

The bi-exponential result should not be interpreted as proof that we measured two distinct physiological processes. For the 7.5-minute recording, the model estimates a long decay time of about 108 minutes, far beyond the 7.4-minute recording. Its estimated asymptote is about 30 bpm, well below the observed final value of 129 bpm. For the three-hour recording, its estimated asymptote is about 42 bpm, also below the observed final value of 64 bpm. These estimates suggest that the long-term behaviour is uncertain and that the bi-exponential model may be extrapolating beyond what the recordings show. The residual plots also show remaining variability, particularly in the three-hour recording.

Overall, the bi-exponential model is the best statistical description among those tested for these recordings, and it is compatible with literature describing fast and slow recovery phases. It won by AICc in both recordings, but its long-term parameter estimates are uncertain. However, because the data do not identify exact exercise and recovery boundaries and the estimated long-term asymptotes are uncertain, we would not claim that it is a definitive physiological model. The results support using it as a candidate for describing the observed declines; a longer recording with a clearly marked end of exercise would be needed to assess the recovery phases and asymptote more reliably.
